21.1.intro: Packing orders yourself is cheap at first, but later it eats your growing time. A 3PL is a warehouse company that stores and ships for you. It makes sense when packing takes more of your week than selling.

steps.say: For one normal week, write down how many orders you sent and how many hours packing, labelling and drop-offs took.
steps.check: You have orders per week and packing hours per week.
steps.lost: Write two numbers: orders and hours.

steps.say: Work out your cost per order today: packaging + labels + postage + your time at a fair hourly rate. Example: $1 + $0.50 + $9 + 10 minutes at $30 an hour ($5) = $15.50.
steps.check: You have one true cost per order, including your time.
steps.lost: Add up box, label, postage and your time.

steps.say: Ask at least 3 warehouses to quote on the same sample month: orders per month, units per order, number of products, carton sizes, and pallets or shelves of stock.
steps.check: You have 3 quotes for the same workload.
steps.careful: Outside the US: in Australia, most warehouses are in the biggest cities, so ask about delivery times to Perth and regional areas. US: one central warehouse reaches most addresses in about 2 to 5 business days by ground. Stock held in a state can create sales tax duties there, so read Lesson 22.3 first.
steps.lost: Ask 3 warehouses for a quote.

steps.say: Compare the full monthly bill, not just pick and pack: receiving, storage (per pallet, shelf or cubic metre), packaging, monthly minimums, set-up, returns handling and peak surcharges.
steps.check: You can see the real total for each quote.
steps.lost: Add every fee for one quote.

steps.say: Ask each warehouse for a sample invoice from a client about your size.
steps.check: You can see fees the price sheet leaves out.
steps.lost: Ask for one sample invoice.

steps.say: Ask 3 service questions: the daily order cut-off time, the error rate they measure, and what they do when they make a mistake.
steps.check: You know how reliable each warehouse is.
steps.lost: Ask: what time is your daily cut-off?

steps.say: Check orders flow in from Shopify by themselves, and tracking flows back.
steps.check: The warehouse connects to your store with no copying by hand.
steps.lost: Ask: do you connect to Shopify?

21.2.intro: Most warehouse moves go wrong in the handover week. A careful switch avoids the usual problems.

steps.say: Give every product and variant its own SKU (your product code) and a barcode before anything ships (Module 13).
steps.check: Every variant has a SKU and barcode.
steps.lost: Give your best seller a SKU.

steps.say: Send a delivery notice with each shipment, listing what's in each carton by SKU and quantity.
steps.check: The warehouse knows what's coming and doesn't charge extra for unlabelled cartons.
steps.lost: List what's in each box.

steps.say: Ask the warehouse to count everything when it arrives and send you the count. Fix gaps before you switch.
steps.check: Their count matches what you sent.
steps.lost: Compare their count with yours.

steps.say: Pick a quiet day to switch. Never the week before a sale.
steps.check: Your switch date is away from any promotion.
steps.lost: Pick a quiet week.

steps.say: Place 3 test orders: one item, several items, and a remote address.
steps.check: All 3 arrive and tracking reaches the customer.
steps.lost: Place one test order.

steps.say:
For the first month, match stock every week.

1. Put the warehouse stock report next to Shopify's **Inventory** page.
2. Ask the warehouse about any gap bigger than a few units.
steps.check: Stock numbers stay in step.
steps.careful: Keep a little stock at home for the first month, so you can send replacements fast.
steps.lost: Compare one product's count each week.

steps.say: Write down who to call when something goes wrong, and how fast they promise to answer.
steps.check: You have a named contact and response time.
steps.lost: Save their phone number.

21.3.intro: Shipping is often one of your biggest costs after the product. Know it before you set prices, and have a plan for delays.

steps.say: Weigh and measure your 3 most common parcels.
steps.check: You know the size and weight of each. Carriers charge by size as well as weight, so smaller boxes can save money.
steps.lost: Weigh your most common parcel.

steps.say: Get prices from at least 2 carriers for your top delivery areas.
steps.check: You can compare prices side by side.
steps.careful: Outside the US: compare the national post with private couriers, especially over 1 kg (in Australia, also for WA and regional areas). US: compare the postal service with private carriers. Ground services are often cheaper for heavy parcels, the postal service for small light ones.
steps.lost: Get 2 quotes for your most common parcel.

steps.say: Work out your average shipping cost per order from last month's invoices. Enter it in Helix under shipping.
steps.check: Helix shows true profit including shipping.
steps.lost: Total shipping ÷ orders. Enter it in Helix.

steps.say: Choose a rule: free shipping over an amount, a flat rate, or real-time rates. Set any free shipping amount a little above your average order (Lesson 14.10).
steps.check: You have one clear shipping rule.
steps.lost: Pick free shipping over a bit more than your average order.

steps.say: Show delivery times on product pages and at checkout.
steps.check: Fewer "where is my order" emails.
steps.lost: Add delivery times to one product page.

steps.say: Write a delay plan: a second carrier you can switch to, an email you can send in minutes, and a store banner.
steps.check: You can react to a postal delay the same day.
steps.careful: US: ship within the time you state, or 30 days if you state none. If you will be late, tell buyers and offer to cancel with a full refund.
steps.lost: Write the delay email now, ready to send.

steps.say: Check carrier prices every time they announce a rise, and at least once a year.
steps.check: Your shipping rates never fall behind your costs.
steps.lost: Put a yearly reminder in your calendar.

21.4.intro: Some parcels go missing or arrive broken. Decide ahead who pays and how fast you fix it.

steps.say: Track lost and damaged parcels for one month: how many, what they cost, and which carrier.
steps.check: You know the monthly cost of lost and damaged parcels.
steps.lost: Write down each lost parcel this month.

steps.say: Write a simple rule. Example: resend or refund once the carrier marks a parcel lost, or the customer sends a photo of damage.
steps.check: Anyone on your team can handle a claim the same way.
steps.lost: Write one sentence: when we resend.

steps.say: Claim from the carrier when you can. Keep proof of value and photos of the packaging.
steps.check: Some of the cost comes back.
steps.lost: Keep photos of broken parcels.

steps.say: If you offer shipping protection (a small fee that covers loss or damage), make it opt-in: unticked by default, with the price shown.
steps.check: Customers choose it. It's never ticked for them.
steps.careful: Outside the US: in Australia, pre-ticked extras must be included in the total price you show. US: the FTC treats hidden or pre-ticked charges as a risk area.
steps.lost: Make sure the box starts unticked.

steps.say: Record protection fees as income, and resends as costs.
steps.check: You can see if protection pays for itself.
steps.lost: Write fees in, resends out.

steps.say: Improve the packaging for anything that breaks more than once.
steps.check: Damage claims fall.
steps.lost: Add padding to the item that breaks most.

21.5.intro: Every return costs you twice: the refund and the handling. Aim for fewer returns and more exchanges, always within the law.

steps.say: Work out your return rate: returned orders ÷ orders for the last 3 months, by product. Example: 12 ÷ 300 = 4%.
steps.check: You have a return rate for each product.
steps.lost: Returns ÷ orders for your best seller.

steps.say: Record a reason for every return (too small, too big, not as pictured, faulty, changed mind). Fix the top reason first.
steps.check: You know your number one return reason.
steps.lost: Write the reason for each return.

steps.say: Stop returns early with a clear size guide, real photos, measurements, and reviews that talk about fit.
steps.check: Product pages answer fit and look questions.
steps.lost: Add measurements to one product.

steps.say: Offer an exchange or store credit first. Keep a refund available where the law needs it.
steps.check: More returns become exchanges.
steps.careful: Outside the US: in Australia, customers have rights to repair, replacement or refund for faulty products, whatever your policy says. Never write "no refunds". "No refunds for change of mind" is fine. UK and EU: online shoppers can usually cancel within 14 days of delivery for any reason. EU: since 19 June 2026 your site also needs a clear "withdraw from contract here" option for those 14 days. US: honour the policy you publish. Some states have their own rules.
steps.lost: Offer an exchange first.

steps.say: Make returns easy to start, with a form or portal. Check the portal's price against how many returns you get.
steps.check: Returns are simple and the tool pays for itself.
steps.lost: Add a simple returns form.

steps.say: Check returned items quickly. Put sellable stock back on sale.
steps.check: Returned stock is sellable again within days.
steps.lost: Check returns the day they arrive.

steps.say: Enter refunds in Helix.
steps.check: Your profit numbers include refunds.
steps.lost: Enter this week's refunds.

21.6.intro: A spreadsheet works for a few products. It breaks with many variants, more than one location, or orders on the way.

steps.say: Start with the Helix **Suppliers & stock** page for reorder points, sell-out dates and order-by dates (Lesson 19.9).
steps.check: Each product shows when to reorder.
steps.lost: Open **Suppliers & stock**.

steps.say: Move to stock software when 2 or more are true: over about 100 variants, more than one warehouse, frequent stock mistakes, or hours each week on stock.
steps.check: You know if you need software yet.
steps.lost: Count how many are true for you.

steps.say: Before you buy, list what you need: purchase orders, landed cost (product plus freight, duties and fees), several locations, bundles, and a link to your accounting.
steps.check: You have a short list of needs.
steps.lost: Write your top 3 needs.

steps.say: Trial the tool with your own data. Check bundles and returns work.
steps.check: The tool handles your real cases.
steps.lost: Try it with one bundle.

steps.say: Count all stock at least once a year (Lesson 23.3). Spot-check best sellers monthly.
steps.check: There's one accurate place for stock numbers.
steps.lost: Count your best seller this month.

21.7.intro: Most questions are the same few: where's my order, can I change size, how do I return this? Fast, friendly answers turn worried buyers into repeat buyers.

steps.say: Read your last 50 customer emails and messages. Group them by question. Count the top five.
steps.check: You have your five most common questions, and how often each comes up.
steps.lost: Read 10 messages. What's asked most?

steps.say: Write a saved reply for each of the five, in your own voice. Put the answers on your FAQ and order confirmation pages too.
steps.check: Five saved replies, and the same answers on your site.
steps.lost: Write one saved reply for "where is my order?"

steps.say: Bring email, chat and social messages into one shared inbox, usually a help desk app. Turn on an automatic order tracking reply.
steps.check: Every message lands in one place, and "where is my order" gets an instant answer. Shopify Inbox covers chat and social messages, not email.
steps.lost: Turn on the automatic tracking reply.

steps.say: Set a reply goal (like within one business day). Check each week how many messages missed it.
steps.check: You know your reply time, and which questions take longest.
steps.careful: Never argue in public replies. Move complaints to private messages fast, fix the problem, then thank the customer publicly.
steps.lost: Aim to reply within one business day.

21.8.intro: Some products must meet safety rules, and a few are banned. If a product hurts someone, you have days to tell the regulator. Check each product once and write your plan before anything goes wrong.

steps.say: List each product and where you sell it. Search the Australian mandatory standards and bans on productsafety.gov.au for each product type.
steps.check: Each product is marked: standard applies, banned, or nothing found.
steps.careful: Button or coin batteries, toys for young children, baby sleep products and furniture that can tip need extra care.
steps.lost: Start with your best seller.

steps.say: Ask your supplier for test reports, labels and instructions for every product a standard covers. Save them in one folder per product.
steps.check: Proof is on file before you sell.
steps.lost: Ask for the test report first.

steps.say: Check labels and listings. Put the same safety warnings in the product description.
steps.check: What people read online matches what arrives.
steps.lost: Copy the box warning into the listing.

steps.say: Selling to the EU? Each listing must show the maker's name, postal and email address, an EU responsible person if the maker is outside the EU, a product picture and ID, and warnings in the customer's language.
steps.check: Every EU listing shows all four. No EU responsible person? Pause EU sales of that product.
steps.lost: Add the maker's details to one listing.

steps.say: Selling to the US? Children's products covered by a CPSC rule need lab testing and a Children's Product Certificate. Other covered products need a General Certificate of Conformity.
steps.check: A certificate is on file for each covered product.
steps.careful: Since 8 July 2026, importers must file certificate data electronically with US Customs.
steps.lost: Ask your supplier if a CPSC rule covers it.

steps.say: Write a one-page incident plan. Any message about an injury, burn, choking or illness goes to one person the same day.
steps.check: One owner, the deadlines and the report links on one page.
steps.careful: Australia: report to the ACCC within 2 days of becoming aware of a death, serious injury or serious illness. If in doubt, report.
steps.lost: Pick who handles injury messages.

steps.say: If a product is unsafe: stop selling it, tell the regulator, email every buyer and offer a refund, repair or replacement.
steps.check: Nobody else can buy it and buyers know what to do.
steps.careful: Australia: tell the ACCC within 2 days of starting a safety recall.
steps.lost: Unpublish the product first.
